notes.meaning: Once the psalmist saw that he needed to change, he acted right away. He did not put it off or keep going back and forth in his mind. When God shows us something to do, it is best to do it now, not "some other time."

Wicked people have tied him up like ropes, or tangled him in their traps. They hurt him because he loves God's law. Even so, he does not forget God's word. No worry or sadness should push it out of our minds or rob us of its comfort.

He is so full of thankfulness that he gets out of bed in the middle of the night to praise God. He does this in private, not to be seen by others. He thanks God for His "righteous judgments," meaning God's fair and right ways and words. Praising God was worth more to him than sleep.

The psalmist loves God's people and spends time with them. He loves them because they honor God and obey Him. Though Henry takes him to be a king, he gladly makes friends with even the poorest person who fears God. Enjoying the company of believers is a sign that you belong to them.

God's kind, faithful love can be seen all over the earth, even among animals and birds. So the psalmist asks for the gift he wants most, to be taught God's ways. If God feeds the birds, surely He will teach His children.
Looking back on his life, the psalmist says God has treated him well, just as He promised. However God has dealt with us, it is better than we deserve, and it is done in love for our good.

"Good judgment" here means a good "taste." It is the ability to tell true from false and right from wrong. He asks for this along with knowledge, because he already trusts God's commands. Many people know a lot but have little good sense, and he wants both.

When life was easy, he drifted away from God like a lost sheep. Then hard times ("affliction") came, and they brought him back to obeying God's word. God often uses trouble like a parent's correction, to call His children home.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible follows the old Greek and Latin and reads "humbled" instead of "afflicted": "Before I was humbled I offended."

notes.meaning: God is good in who He is, and He does good in what He does. The goodness the psalmist most wants from Him is to be taught His ways. Then he too can be good and do good.
Proud people have spread lies about him. The word pictures them smearing false paint over his real character. He does not strike back. He just keeps obeying God with his whole heart.

Their hearts are like hearts covered in thick fat. Their comfort and pride have made them dull and unfeeling toward God. In contrast, the psalmist finds real joy in God's law. He would not trade places with them.
He can honestly say his suffering was good for him. It humbled him, softened his heart and taught him God's ways in a way nothing else had. The God who corrected him was also teaching him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible, following the old Latin, reads "humbled" here as well: "thou hast humbled me."

notes.meaning: God's word is worth more to him than piles of gold and silver. So whatever he lost in his troubles, he gained more by learning God's law. If he valued it so highly with only part of the Bible, we have even more reason to treasure it.

God made him with His own hands. So the psalmist asks the One who made him to also give him understanding. Then he can learn God's commands and live for what he was made for. Sin has made us unfit to serve God, so we need Him to make us new.

He hopes that other believers will be glad when they see him. They will see that trusting God's promise did not let him down. When God helps one of His people, it encourages all the others to trust Him too.

He admits that God's dealings with him are right, even the painful ones. God let him suffer out of faithfulness, like a loving father correcting a child for his good. It is easy to say God is fair in general, but harder when it is your own trouble.
Even after accepting God's correction, he asks for comfort from God's kind, faithful love. He leans on God's promise. Since God has promised kindness to His servants, he can boldly ask for it.

He asks for God's tender mercy, like the tender love of a father or mother, so that he may truly live. Without the sense of God's favor he felt as if he were dead. He reminds God that His law is his joy.
Proud people have treated him wrongly with lies, for no good reason. He asks God to bring them to shame. But he does not let it upset him. He keeps thinking on God's ways.

He longs for the friendship of other believers, especially those who know God's word well. Some may have doubted him during his troubles. He hopes they will come back to him and be encouraged by what God has done for him.
He prays for a heart that is truly whole and honest toward God's ways, not just outward show. He wants to love and obey God sincerely and steadily. Then he will not end up ashamed.

He has longed so long for God to rescue him that he feels worn out. Yet he keeps hoping in God's promise. Henry adds that it can also be heard as the longing of Old Testament believers for the coming Savior.

His eyes are tired from watching for God to keep His promise. He cries, "When will You comfort me?" God's help may take a long time to come. When our eyes grow tired, our faith still must not give up.

In those days bottles were made of animal skin. One hung in a smoky tent became black, dry and shriveled, and was cast aside as useless. That is how worn down he felt in body and mind. Yet even then he did not forget God's ways.
He asks how long he must wait. His life is short, so he hopes God will act soon. He does not ask for the power to take revenge himself. He asks God, the fair Judge, to deal with those who hurt him.

His proud enemies have dug pits for him, like hunters trapping animals. That means they plotted against him with careful, sneaky plans. Such things go against God's law, which forbids planning harm to a neighbor.
People may be false, but every one of God's commands is true and can be trusted. He is attacked for no reason, so he cries out simply, "Help me!" He trusts that God will rescue His people.
His enemies nearly destroyed him. Still, he never turned away from God's ways. He would rather lose everything than let go of God's word.

He asks God to "revive" him, which means to give him new life and strength. He asks this because of God's loving kindness, not because he has earned it. Only with this new life can he keep obeying. The surest sign of God's love for us is His good work inside us.
